form.label: Advanced Workshop #2 — Correlation
form.description: Splunk-side proof that one Collector, two destinations, and one log line carry everything needed to pivot into APM.

div.p: One OpenTelemetry Collector fans data out to two destinations — Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Observability Cloud. A single log line is pivot-able from APM the moment it carries trace_id, service.name, and deployment.environment together — this dashboard proves that correlation holds, and that severity classification actually works, on the Splunk side.

div.style: background:#FFF8E1; border-left:5px solid #F1813F; padding:10px 18px; border-radius:4px; margin-top:8px;
div.p: Fills in during Advanced Workshop #2. The workshop app installs every dashboard at once in Foundational Workshop #2, so this one is here early. Until you fan the Collector out to a second destination, its panels are empty — that is expected, not a fault.

panel.title: % of ALL Log Events Carrying trace_id — Expected to Be Small
panel.description: This is a traffic-mix ratio, not a health signal — do not read a low number here as broken. Only application log lines carry trace_id (via logback); Tomcat access-log lines never do, and access logs vastly outnumber application logs under normal load. The App Log vs Access Log Split panel below shows the same split with both populations labeled. For the metric that DOES have a "good=high" direction, see "% of Application-Layer Logs Carrying trace_id" elsewhere in this row — same field, filtered to just the application-log population.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs | stats count as total, count(eval(isnotnull(trace_id) AND trace_id!="")) as with_trace | eval value=round((with_trace/total)*100,1) | table value
index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs | stats count as total, count(eval(isnotnull(severity))) as classified | eval value=round((classified/total)*100,1) | table value

panel.title: % of Application-Layer Logs Carrying trace_id
panel.description: Same field, different denominator: this filters to application log lines only (identified by the ISO-8601 logback timestamp, excluding Tomcat access-log lines) before computing coverage. Unlike the all-events figure to the left, this one SHOULD read close to 100% — a drop here means the correlation transform itself has stopped working, not that access-log traffic changed shape.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs | eval is_app_log=if(match(_raw,"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T"),1,0) | where is_app_log=1 | stats count as total, count(eval(isnotnull(trace_id) AND trace_id!="")) as with_trace | eval value=round((with_trace/total)*100,1) | table value
index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs trace_id=* severity=* | stats count as value | table value

panel.title: Severity Classification Coverage Over Time — Written at Ingest, Not Retroactive

search.query: index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs | eval s=if(isnull(severity),"UNKNOWN","classified") | timechart span=$span_token$ count by s

panel.title: Single-Event Correlation Proof (Most Recent 15)
panel.description: Each row is one Splunk Enterprise log event that already carries trace_id, service.name, and deployment.environment together. This is exactly what makes the APM service map's "Logs" pivot work: Log Observer Connect (or a manual search) can jump straight from a trace in APM to this event, and back, because the correlating fields already live on the same event — no join, no lookup, no extra pipeline required.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs trace_id=* | rename "service.name" as svc, "deployment.environment" as env | sort -_time | head 15 | table trace_id, severity, svc, env, host

panel.title: Application Log vs Access Log Split (Expected Partial trace_id Coverage)
panel.description: trace_id is auto-extracted only from application log lines that pass through logback. Tomcat access-log lines never carry a trace_id — that is expected and correct, not a bug. This split shows both populations side by side.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs | eval has_trace=if(isnotnull(trace_id) AND trace_id!="","app log (has trace_id)","access log (no trace_id)") | stats count by has_trace

div.h2: All Three Signals, One Platform — What Correlation Actually Buys You
div.p: Everything above proves the correlating trace_id field exists. The panels below use it. By this point in the workshop your single Collector is shipping logs, metrics and traces into Splunk Enterprise simultaneously — so the same production incident can be counted, timed and dissected three independent ways in one search bar.

The recurring lesson: when three lenses agree, you trust the number. When they diverge, the divergence is itself the finding — it means sampling, dropping, or misrouting somewhere in the pipeline, and it is only visible because all three signals landed in the same place.

panel.title: One Incident, Three Signals, One Timeline
panel.description:
Log events (blue) and spans (purple) are counted from the event indexes; node CPU load (orange, right-hand axis) comes from the metric index. Three separate pipelines, three separate storage engines, one time axis. Under normal load the log and span curves track each other at a fixed ratio — one request produces a roughly constant number of log lines and spans. Watch for shape changes: if spans flatten while logs keep climbing, the trace pipeline is sampling or dropping; if both drop while CPU stays high, the Collector — not the application — is the thing that stopped. Use the Time Granularity dropdown at the top of the page to change bucket size.
Kept as a line chart, unlike most panels in this app: Spans and Log Events differ by roughly 20x in volume, and an area fill for Spans buries the much smaller Log Events series almost entirely — tested live, not assumed. Three lines at different scales is still imprecise, but nothing gets visually occluded, which matters here since the whole point of this panel is watching both curves' shapes together.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs OR index=k8s_ws_traces | eval signal=if(index=="k8s_ws_traces","Spans","Log Events") | timechart span=$span_token$ count by signal | append [| mstats avg(_value) as cl WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics metric_name="system.cpu.load_average.1m" span=$span_token$] | stats sum("Log Events") as "Log Events" sum("Spans") as "Spans" avg(cl) as cl by _time | eval "Node CPU Load (1m)"=round(cl,2) | fields - cl

panel.title: The Same Failures, Counted Three Different Ways
panel.description: Three independent measurements of one underlying population of failed requests: the Tomcat access log counting HTTP 5xx responses, the application log counting ERROR-severity lines emitted by logback, and the trace pipeline counting spans stamped STATUS_CODE_ERROR. Nothing in the pipeline forces these to agree — they are produced by different instrumentation, exported by different Collector pipelines, and stored in different indexes. Reading the result: agreement within a few percent means every pipeline is healthy end to end. A single lens reading materially LOW is the interesting case — it points at that specific pipeline (trace sampling, a dropped log source, a misrouted exporter), not at the application. A lens reading HIGH usually means it counts something broader than the others, for example retries or internal errors that never reached the user.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs OR index=k8s_ws_traces | eval is_app_log=if(match(_raw,"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T"),1,0) | rename "status.code" as status_code | eval lens=case( index=="k8s_ws_petclinic_logs" AND is_app_log=0 AND http_status>=500, "1. Access log — HTTP 5xx responses", index=="k8s_ws_petclinic_logs" AND is_app_log=1 AND severity=="ERROR", "2. Application log — ERROR severity lines", index=="k8s_ws_traces" AND status_code=="STATUS_CODE_ERROR", "3. Traces — spans with STATUS_CODE_ERROR") | where isnotnull(lens) | stats count as Errors by lens | eventstats max(Errors) as m | eval divergence=round(((Errors-m)/m)*100,1) | fields - m | rename lens as "Signal / Lens", divergence as "Divergence vs Highest Lens"

panel.title: Log → Trace Pivot Success Rate (Higher Is Better)
panel.description: Of the log events that carry a trace_id, this is the percentage whose trace_id actually resolves to at least one span in the trace index for the same window. This one DOES have a good/bad direction: high is good. It is the direct measure of whether "click the trace_id in a log line and land on the trace" will work for an on-call engineer. Anything well below 100% means spans are being sampled away, dropped by the Collector, or exported to a destination this Splunk instance cannot see — the log is telling you a trace exists when it does not. A few percent of misses at the window edges is normal: a request that started just before the window can have its log line inside the range and its span outside it.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_traces OR (index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs trace_id=*) | eval src=if(index=="k8s_ws_traces","trace","log") | stats count(eval(src=="log")) as logcnt, count(eval(src=="trace")) as trcnt by trace_id | stats count(eval(logcnt>0)) as with_log, count(eval(logcnt>0 AND trcnt>0)) as both | eval value=round((both/with_log)*100,1) | table value

panel.title: Trace-to-Log Join Proof — Every Distinct trace_id, Classified
panel.description: Every distinct trace_id seen anywhere in the window, bucketed by which signals actually contain it. "Span only" is the expected majority and is NOT a defect — the application emits a log line for a subset of requests, but the agent traces all of them, so most traces legitimately have no matching log. "Log only" is the row that matters: a log line advertising a trace_id with no span behind it is a broken pivot, and this count should stay near zero. "Fully correlated" is the population where a responder can move freely between the log line and the full request waterfall shown below.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_traces OR (index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs trace_id=*) | eval src=if(index=="k8s_ws_traces","trace","log") | stats dc(src) as n, values(src) as srcs by trace_id | eval class=case( n=2, "Fully correlated — span AND log line both present", srcs=="trace", "Span only — no application log line emitted (expected majority)", srcs=="log", "Log only — advertised trace_id has no span (broken pivot)") | stats count as Traces by class | eventstats sum(Traces) as tot | eval share=round((Traces/tot)*100,1) | fields - tot | sort 0 -Traces | rename class as "Correlation Class", share as "Share of Distinct trace_id"

panel.title: Ingest Mix — What Each Signal Actually Costs You in Volume
panel.description: Relative volume of everything the Collector delivered to Splunk Enterprise in this window: log events and spans counted from the event indexes, metric data points counted from the metric indexes. This is the practical input to every cost and retention conversation — traces are almost always the largest single contributor because one user request fans out into a dozen spans, and infrastructure metrics scale with cluster size rather than with traffic. No colour scale here on purpose: high volume is neither good nor bad, it is a budget fact. The lever it points at is span sampling and metric collection interval, not turning a signal off.

search.query: | tstats count as items WHERE index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs OR index=k8s_ws_traces BY index | append [| mstats count(_value) as items WHERE index=k8s_ws_petclinic_metrics OR index=k8s_ws_metrics metric_name=* BY index] | eval Signal=case( index=="k8s_ws_petclinic_logs", "Logs — application + access", index=="k8s_ws_traces", "Traces — spans", index=="k8s_ws_petclinic_metrics", "Metrics — application (JVM, JDBC)", index=="k8s_ws_metrics", "Metrics — infrastructure + Collector self-telemetry") | stats sum(items) as Items by Signal index | eventstats sum(Items) as tot | eval share=round((Items/tot)*100,1) | fields - tot | sort 0 -Items | rename index as "Splunk Index", Items as "Events / Data Points", share as "Share of Ingest"

panel.title: One Request, End to End — The Deepest Live Trace in This Window
panel.description: This panel picks the richest trace in the selected window automatically — no trace_id is hardcoded, so it works for every participant and refreshes with the time picker. Every row shares one trace_id, and parent_span_id chains them into the call tree: the SPAN_KIND_SERVER row is the inbound HTTP request, INTERNAL rows are Spring repository and Hibernate session calls, and CLIENT rows are the actual JDBC round trips with the SQL text attached. Start Offset is measured from the first span of the trace, so reading down the offset column reconstructs the waterfall — this is how you find the one slow database call inside an otherwise fast request. That whole structure is recovered from a single 32-character identifier, the same one printed on the log lines in the panels above.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_traces | eventstats count as spans by trace_id | eventstats max(spans) as maxspans | where spans=maxspans | sort 0 -_time | eventstats first(trace_id) as pick | where trace_id=pick | eventstats min(start_time) as t0 | eval offset_ms=round((start_time-t0)/1000000,2), dur_ms=round((end_time-start_time)/1000000,2) | rename "status.code" as status, "attributes.db.statement" as sql | eval kind=replace(kind,"SPAN_KIND_",""), status=replace(status,"STATUS_CODE_","") | eval sql=if(isnull(sql),"—",if(len(sql)>110,substr(sql,1,110)." …",sql)) | sort 0 +start_time | table trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id, name, kind, status, offset_ms, dur_ms, sql | rename trace_id as "Trace ID", span_id as "Span ID", parent_span_id as "Parent Span ID", name as "Span Name", kind as "Kind", status as "Status", offset_ms as "Start Offset (ms)", dur_ms as "Duration (ms)", sql as "SQL Statement"
